transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-02
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Park (Redwood AE), Ravi Shah (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Aurora Head of ML), Ethan Price (Aurora CTO), Luis Ortega (Aurora Platform), Zoe Tan (Product)

Summary:
Short demo of Redwood structured output (JSON mode), function/tool calling, and Console/Optimize features. Focus on schemas, guardrails, and how to enforce structured outputs for downstream tool orchestration. Customer interested in Dedicated vs Hosted, security, and integration with existing event pipelines.

Topics:
- Structured output: JSON mode + strict schemas
- Function & tool calling (examples: ticket create, enrichment calls)
- Guardrails and validation errors handling
- Console observability and Optimize suggestions (batching/quantization)
- Deployment options: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private/VPC

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jamie Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jamie, AE on the Redwood team, with Ravi our SE. Today we'll run through structured output JSON mode and function calling, demo in the Console and API. 
[00:12] Maya Chen: Hi, thanks. High level — we're evaluating for our customer support pipeline, need deterministic JSON outputs for downstream automation. Latency and cost are constraints.
[00:25] Ravi Shah: Totally. We'll show the JSON schema enforcement and how we surface validation errors and fallback. Also the Console has a structured-output mode where you can paste schemas and test sample prompts.
[00:40] Ethan Price: Quick question — how strict is "strict"? If model deviates, do we retry or fail? We have event processors that expect a specific schema.
[00:53] Ravi Shah: Good Q. Redwood supports three behaviors: strict validation that returns an error (you can catch and retry), auto-correct with a constrained parsing pass, or a sanitized fallback to a simpler schema. In the API you set the policy per route. We'll demo strict and auto-correct.
[01:12] Luis Ortega: And for function calls — can the model call our internal enrichment service directly or do we route via Redwood tooling?
[01:22] Jamie Park: The function/tool calling is two parts: the model returning a structured payload we map to a function signature, and the runtime invoking an HTTP webhook or internal tool. For Hosted we can call webhooks. For Dedicated/Private you can run tool connectors inside your VPC.
[01:35] Zoe Tan: Sounds good. Security wise, we'd need audit logs and KMS integration.
[01:41] Ravi Shah: We have audit logs per request and KMS support for Private. We'll include the SOC2 excerpt in the follow-up.
[01:52] Jamie Park: Ok demo time — switching to Console. I'm going to paste a sample schema for a ticket creation intent: ticket_id string, priority enum low/med/high, issue_summary string, tags array[string], customer_id string.
[02:07] Ravi Shah: Watch as I send a chat prompt in JSON mode. Console shows the schema on the right and a live validator. We're using Redwood's "json_mode": "strict" flag here.
[02:22] [screen share noises] 
[02:30] Ravi Shah: Example prompt: "Customer says: My account's been charged twice, please refund." Model returns a payload that includes html-escaped text sometimes — you'll see the validator rejecting because ticket_id was missing.
[02:46] Maya Chen: Does the validator give structured error messages we can programmatically parse?
[02:52] Ravi Shah: Yes — error includes field path, expected type, and confidence score. We also expose a normalized error code.
[03:05] Ethan Price: If we run at scale, what's the perf hit of strict validation?
[03:11] Ravi Shah: Minimal for simple schemas, under 5% latency increase for typical ticket schemas. For very deep nested schemas we recommend using the Optimize suggestions: lighter quantization + larger batch sizes for throughput.
[03:26] Luis Ortega: Can we pre-validate with sampling on Console to surface hard edge cases?
[03:31] Ravi Shah: Yes, Console has a sample-run tool that runs N prompts against the route and summarizes validation failures.
[03:40] Jamie Park: Next, function calling. I'm going to show a demo where the model returns a function call object: {"function":"create_ticket","args":{...}}. Our runtime maps that to a webhook we configured.
[03:55] [keyboard click] 
[04:00] Ravi Shah: In this example the model attempted to call create_ticket but returned tags as a comma-separated string instead of array. Because we supplied a schema for args, the runtime flagged it and ran the auto-correct pass which coerced into array and added a warning field.
[04:16] Maya Chen: That auto-correct is useful, but we want to avoid silent fixes in some flows. Can we configure to surface warnings only in staging?
[04:26] Ravi Shah: Absolutely. Policies are per-route and you can set environment overrides. Staging can be "warn-only" while prod is "strict-fail".
[04:36] Ethan Price: For Dedicated, is the webhook call still proxied through Redwood? We need internal network access policies.
[04:44] Jamie Park: For Dedicated you can run connectors inside your VPC, so the calls stay internal. Hosted can use signed webhooks.
[04:51] Luis Ortega: Any limits on function call size? We have large metadata.
[04:56] Ravi Shah: Payloads up to several MB are supported but we recommend passing references and letting backend enrichment fetch blobs. Optimize can suggest batching or pointer patterns to reduce token cost.
[05:10] [ambient chatter — people typing]
[05:25] Jamie Park: Quick aside on guardrails: we support pre-output token filters and post-output schema validation. Pre-output filters drop unsafe content and post-output validator checks shape.
[05:39] Zoe Tan: Does pre-output filtering affect embeddings or reranking?
[05:44] Ravi Shah: Not for embeddings; it's for generation and structured outputs. For reranking we have separate heuristics.
[05:50] Jamie Park: I'm going to open the API example — here's a cURL that calls /v1/generate with schema parameter and json_mode=strict. You can see headers include x-redwood-route and route policy.
[06:05] [brief pause] 
[06:12] Ravi Shah: Now we'll demo an end-to-end where model calls two tools: enrichment_service then ticket_create. The runtime orchestrates calls and shows a trace in Console with per-tool latency and per-token cost.
[06:28] Ethan Price: We need per-customer cost attribution — can Console break down token cost by route and by customer_id?
[06:36] Jamie Park: Yes — Console has token-level breakdown and tags, you can tag requests by customer_id or internal request_id and slice costs.
[06:44] Maya Chen: For POC, we care about latency p95 and error budget. What's realistic for a ticket creation flow?
[06:52] Ravi Shah: With Dedicated and modest batching you can hit p95 under 300ms for short responses. Hosted averages depend on model size — for medium models p95 ~ 400-600ms. We'll provide benchmarks.
[07:05] Luis Ortega: On monitoring — do we get traces to our APM?
[07:09] Jamie Park: Yes, Redwood can forward traces and we have tracing hooks for Datadog/New Relic.
[07:16] [10 minute skip — paraphrased exchange about pricing model and commit levels] 
[18:20] Ethan Price: Clarify: Dedicated pricing is per-GPU pool commit? Do we get burst?
[18:27] Jamie Park: Yes commits are monthly, with burst credits and autoscale policies. We'll share the pricing sheet.
[18:36] Maya Chen: Questions on security checklist — SSO, RBAC, KMS, audit log retention.
[18:42] Ravi Shah: We support SAML SSO, granular RBAC in Console, KMS integration for Private, and audit log exports to S3 for retention.
[18:55] Zoe Tan: Any compliance references?
[18:58] Jamie Park: We'll attach SOC2 and our compliance pack in the follow-up.
[19:05] [Ravi runs a short sample-run in Console showing 50 test prompts and a failure breakdown] 
[19:20] Ravi Shah: Results: 50 prompts, 6 schema validation failures. Most were malformed dates and one missing required customer_id. Console suggests adding a date parser pre-step or nullable field.
[19:34] Maya Chen: Can Optimize suggest a quantization profile? We run 24/7 and want cost savings without regression.
[19:40] Ravi Shah: Optimize will suggest quantize-to-8-bit for candidate models, caching of common prefixes, and batching configs. We can run an offline eval to estimate quality delta.
[19:52] Ethan Price: We'll need a regression budget — acceptable drop in QA or F1 metric.
[19:57] Jamie Park: We'll help set up eval harness that runs against your golden set.
[20:04] [later in call — discussion of error handling patterns and example code snippets] 
[34:10] Ravi Shah: Code snippet: if response.validation_error -> log, increment metric, if policy==auto-correct use corrected_payload else raise 422 to caller.
[34:22] Luis Ortega: We want circuit-breakers around downstream webhooks.
[34:27] Ravi Shah: Redwood runtime supports retries with backoff and dead-letter routing.
[34:33] Maya Chen: Great. For the POC, we'd want: 1) route with strict validation in prod, 2) staging warn-only with auto-correct, 3) sample-run results for top 10 intents.
[34:45] Jamie Park: Sounds good. Next steps we'll capture — pricing, security docs, sample schema + demo repo, and schedule the infra deep dive.
[34:56] Ethan Price: Can you include a simple webhook connector example?
[35:01] Ravi Shah: Yes, I'll add one in the demo repo.
[35:06] Zoe Tan: One more — if model hallucinated PII into ticket summary, do we have a scrubber?
[35:12] Ravi Shah: We have post-process scrubbing and redaction rules, plus token filters pre-output. We'll include examples.
[35:22] Jamie Park: Alright we'll wrap. Thanks all.
[35:26] Maya Chen: Thanks, that was helpful. We'll gather sample data and follow-up.
